P1-W01-M1.title: The same 32 bits, four different agreements
P1-W01-M1.alt: One 32-bit word drawn as four byte cells reading 01000001 01000010 01000011 01000100, with four arrows fanning right to four boxes that read the identical bits as a signed int, an unsigned int, an IEEE-754 float and four ASCII characters. Below, the same four bytes are drawn in the order they actually sit in memory on an arm64 Mac (44 43 42 41), with the big-endian ordering crossed out in red.

P1-W01-M2.title: cc hello.c is four programs, and each leaves a file
P1-W01-M2.alt: Five file chips in a row — hello.c, hello.i, hello.s, hello.o and hello — joined by four arrows labelled cpp, clang -S, clang -c and ld, with the measured byte count under each file. A red crossed-out box denies that compilation is one step. Below, an nm listing shows _main defined and _printf unresolved, and a tall stack of bands draws the resulting process address space from __PAGEZERO up to the stack.

P1-W01-M3.title: The frame dies. The heap block does not.
P1-W01-M3.alt: Two panels of the same call shape. On the left, make_buf returns a pointer to a 32-byte heap block; the make_buf frame is crossed out but a green arrow shows the block still alive and now owned by main. On the right, c() returns the address of a local int z; the frame is crossed out in red and the pointer in main now aims at bytes the next call will reuse. Below, the measured stack budget and a struct-padding comparison of 24 versus 16 bytes.

P1-W01-M4.title: Measured, on a log-log axis: the curves separate where the counts said
P1-W01-M4.alt: A hand-drawn log-log plot of sorting time against array size. A green merge-sort line of slope 1.06 and a blue qsort line of slope 1.11 run almost parallel, with qsort 1.75 times slower; a red selection-sort line of slope 1.95 climbs far more steeply and is continued as a dashed extrapolation off the top of the chart. An inset shows insertion sort at 1700 nanoseconds beating merge sort at n equals 96, and a crossed-out box denies that big-O tells you which algorithm is faster.

P1-W01-M5.title: One symptom, one tool. Guessing is what the other tools are for.
P1-W01-M5.alt: A five-row routing table: each symptom on the left — will not compile, crashes, wrong answer with no crash, fine at -O0 but broken at -O2, memory corruption — points by arrow to the single tool that diagnoses it. On the right, AddressSanitizer's shadow bytes fa fa 05 fa are drawn as cells with 05 highlighted, and three bars compare 65 ms plain, 179 ms with sanitizers and 180 ms at -O0. A crossed-out box rejects scattering printf calls, and an lldb backtrace shows frame one highlighted as the first line you wrote.

P1-W02-M1.title: One command = fork, exec, wait (and everything is inherited)
P1-W02-M1.alt: A shell command box above the six things the shell does before your program starts. To the right, the parent process forks a child, an arrow trying to send an environment change back up is crossed out in red, and the child's three inherited file descriptors show only stdout redirected to a file. Below, the nine permission bits are drawn as a three-by-three grid mapping rwxr-x--- to octal 750, and the child's exit status 1 returns to the parent as dollar-question-mark.

P1-W02-M2.title: Same log, same answer: shape beats tuning by 4.9x
P1-W02-M2.alt: One 1 GB access log feeding two pipelines. The upper five-stage pipeline sorts 8.9 million records before aggregating and takes 135.4 seconds; the lower two-stage pipeline builds a histogram in a single awk pass and takes 27.7 seconds. Beside them, two bars show LC_ALL=C sorting in 20.4 seconds against 86.2 seconds in the default locale, a small branching tree shows catastrophic regex backtracking growing from 37 ms to 31.3 seconds, and a chain of five piped greps is crossed out in red.

P1-W02-M3.title: Three things kill a script. Each has exactly one defence.
P1-W02-M3.alt: A backup.sh box in the centre attacked from three sides: an unquoted variable that word-splits into two tokens, two scheduled copies starting at the same time, and a SIGTERM arriving mid-write. Beside each attack the fix is drawn in green — quoting the variable, an atomic mkdir lock, and write-to-temp-then-rename. Below, a crossed-out trap for SIGKILL and a three-run idempotence checklist where runs two and three must change nothing.

P1-W02-M4.title: A commit is a snapshot. A branch is a sticky note.
P1-W02-M4.alt: On the left, Git's object model: a commit box pointing to a tree pointing to a blob, with the blob's SHA-1 computed by hand from the header and content and matching git rev-parse. On the right, the same starting graph resolved two ways — merge produces a commit M with two parents and rewrites nothing, while rebase replays D and E as new commits D-prime and E-prime and leaves the originals crossed out in red but recoverable through the reflog. A shrinking bar ladder shows git bisect closing 200 commits in eight test runs.

P1-W02-M5.title: The private key never crosses the wire
P1-W02-M5.alt: A laptop holding a 387-byte ed25519 private key and a server holding the 86-byte public key. Three numbered arrows show the server sending a challenge, the laptop signing it, and the server verifying the signature; a fourth arrow labelled 'send the private key' is crossed out in red. Below, known_hosts records the server's own key on a trust-on-first-use basis, and a port-forward runs from localhost:15432 through a bastion to a Postgres on a private subnet, with a direct route from the internet crossed out.

P1-W03-M1.title: A name is a sticky note. Assignment moves the note.
P1-W03-M1.alt: Two sticky notes labelled a and b both point at one list object with refcount 2 and cells 1, 2, 3 and a dashed 4 appended through a. Beside it, the picture most people hold — two separate list objects — is crossed out in red, and the contrasting case a = a + [4] is drawn as a genuinely new object. Below, the CPython object header is drawn field by field with measured sizes, and six bars compare per-record memory for a million records from 268 bytes in a dict down to 28 bytes columnar.

P1-W03-M2.title: The container you pick chooses the exponent
P1-W03-M2.alt: A row of list cells scanned one at a time for a linear membership test, beside a set drawn as eight hash slots where one hash jump lands directly on the answer, with 367867x written between them. Below, list.insert(0) shuffles every element right at 311 microseconds while deque.appendleft writes one pointer in 16 nanoseconds. At the bottom a generator pipeline carries one record at a time and peaks at 14.3 MB, against a list holding all 12.2 million records at 10 499 MB, crossed out in red.

P1-W03-M3.title: An exception rises until something can do anything about it
P1-W03-M3.alt: A four-frame call stack with main at the top and read_file at the bottom. A red zigzag starts in read_file, passes straight through load_user, which is drawn dashed and annotated as having no except clause, and stops at handle_request where a green box turns it into a 404. A bare except Exception: pass frame is crossed out. On the right, try, except, else and finally are drawn as four bands with finally circled, a with-block whose __exit__ the raising body still passes through, and bars comparing an emitted log call at 3.47 microseconds with a filtered one at 0.068.

P1-W03-M4.title: obj.x : the data descriptor wins before the instance dict is read
P1-W03-M4.alt: A flowchart of Python attribute lookup: walk the MRO, and if the name is a data descriptor with __set__ call its __get__ immediately, otherwise check the instance dict, then non-data descriptors, then plain class attributes, then __getattr__. A recursive @property is crossed out in red as a RecursionError. Beside it the three method kinds and what each receives, a diamond inheritance graph with its C3 order D B C A object, and bars showing attribute reads at 4.6, 4.4, 12.8 and 49.6 nanoseconds.

P1-W03-M5.title: Examples test what you thought of. Properties test what you did not.
P1-W03-M5.alt: Two dartboards. The left one, labelled example tests, has three darts clustered in one small region and vast empty board around them, with a note that all three pass at 100% line coverage while the code is still wrong. The right one, labelled property tests, is peppered with thirty-two scattered cases and one circled in red at (2, 3). Between them an arrow reads 'hypothesis: 500 examples, then SHRINK', and below, a descending ladder shrinks (872341, 617) down to the minimal failing case (2, 3).

P1-W04-M1.title: One key, four threads: what the GIL actually costs
P1-W04-M1.alt: Four thread boxes reaching for a single hachured key labelled GIL, with only one holding it. Beside them, one core interleaving jobs A B C D versus four cores running A, B, C and D genuinely at once. Below, a two-by-four grid of measured results shows threads making a CPU-bound workload 0.86 times as fast, circled in red, while asyncio makes an I/O-bound workload 27.02 times faster, circled in green. An Amdahl curve shows 95% parallel code flattening at about 16.8x even on a hundred cores.

P1-W04-M2.title: Something happened between the READ and the WRITE
P1-W04-M2.alt: Two thread timelines interleaved: thread A reads 5, thread B reads 5, both add one, both write 6, and the shared counter ends at 6 instead of 7 — one update lost. Below, the same sequence held by a lock runs uninterrupted while B is blocked and the counter reaches 7. A two-lock deadlock cycle is drawn beside its fix of a fixed lock order, and a producer-queue-consumer design removes the shared state entirely.

P1-W04-M3.title: A pool buys real cores and charges a toll on every task
P1-W04-M3.alt: A parent process fanning work through a dashed pickle toll booth out to four child processes, each drawn with its own GIL. Bars compare worker startup at 54 ms for spawn, 43.2 ms for forkserver and 3.8 ms for fork. A crossover curve shows the pool below break-even until about 100 000 iterations of work per task, with the losing region hachured in red, and a sketch shows eight workers each spawning eleven BLAS threads onto eleven cores.

P1-W04-M4.title: await hands control back, so the loop can run someone else
P1-W04-M4.alt: Four blocking requests drawn as a staircase totalling 200 ms beside four async requests overlapping into about 50 ms. The event loop is drawn as a four-box cycle: run ready callbacks, fire due timers, block in select until I/O is ready, wake the tasks whose futures resolved. A suspended task card notes that its locals are still alive, and a box containing time.sleep and requests.get is crossed out as blocking the loop. Bars show sequential 2.184 s against asyncio gather 0.081 s, and a semaphore ladder from 19 to 4799 requests per second.

P1-W04-M5.title: Retry storms are self-inflicted. Jitter, a bucket and a breaker.
P1-W04-M5.alt: Two timelines: without jitter a thousand retries land in one dense column exactly one second after the upstream failed and knock it over again; with full jitter the same retries are spread across the window and the upstream stays up. Below, the backoff formula with uniform(0, ...) circled, a token bucket metering eight tokens a second, a three-state circuit breaker, and bars comparing a naive client at 285 of 400 in 0.16 s, a retrying client at 358 of 400 with 185 rate-limit errors, and a bucketed client at 400 of 400 with none.

a01-stack-heap.title: Stack, heap, and the pointer that outlived its frame
a01-stack-heap.alt: Three stack frames drawn as boxes on the left and a heap allocation on the right. A green arrow shows make_buf returning a pointer; the make_buf frame is then crossed out in red, and a red arrow shows the caller still holding the address of memory whose owning frame is gone.

a03-binary-search.title: Binary search: the window halving, four rows deep
a03-binary-search.alt: Four rows of the same twelve-element sorted array. In each row the eliminated half is greyed and crossed out, the midpoint is highlighted, and the invariant lo and hi plus the comparison made is written to the right, ending when the midpoint lands on 72.

a05-git-dag.title: Merge versus rebase on the same commit graph
a05-git-dag.alt: The same five-commit graph drawn twice. On the left a merge commit joins the branch back with two parents, preserving the true shape of history. On the right the branch commits are replayed as C-prime and D-prime with new hashes onto a linear history, with a red warning crossed across it about rebasing shared branches.

a07-blocking-vs-async.title: Blocking versus async: the same three requests
a07-blocking-vs-async.alt: Two timelines. The blocking one runs three requests end to end, each mostly a red waiting-on-I/O bar, finishing at 900 milliseconds with the CPU busy 0.7 percent of the time. The async one starts all three within 52 milliseconds and finishes at 310 milliseconds using exactly the same six milliseconds of CPU.

a12-btree-vs-scan.title: B-tree lookup versus a full table scan
a12-btree-vs-scan.alt: Above, a four-level B-tree descent from a root page to the leaf holding row 84,213, taking four page reads and 0.4 milliseconds. Below, the same query as a full scan drawn as twenty-two red page bars with the one matching page in green, costing 6,181 page reads and 340 milliseconds — 850 times slower.

a15-memory-hierarchy.title: The memory hierarchy, with the latencies written in
a15-memory-hierarchy.alt: Seven hachured bars, log-scaled, running from a one-nanosecond L1 cache hit to a ten-millisecond disk seek, each labelled with its real latency and with a human-scale equivalent on the right showing that if an L1 hit took one second, a disk seek would take four months.

a18-gradient-descent.title: Gradient descent, and the learning rate that blew up
a18-gradient-descent.alt: On the left a ball rolls down a hand-drawn loss bowl in five numbered steps that get shorter as the slope flattens, at a learning rate of 0.05. On the right the same bowl at a learning rate of 0.9 sends the ball bouncing further up the walls each step; the panel is crossed out in red and annotated loss 4.1 to 9.8 to 61 to NaN.

a28-backprop.title: Backpropagation through a tiny graph
a28-backprop.alt: A five-node computation graph drawn left to right in blue for the forward pass with the intermediate values written above each node, and long green arrows running right to left underneath carrying the partial derivatives, ending in a weight update that moves w from 3.0 to 2.2.

a32-attention.title: Self-attention: the matrix and the causal mask
a32-attention.alt: A four-by-four attention matrix for the sentence 'the cat sat down'. Each cell in the lower triangle carries its post-softmax weight, hachured more densely where the weight is larger; the upper triangle is crossed out in red and enclosed by a heavy red staircase labelled causal mask, showing that each token can attend only to itself and the tokens before it.

a35-lora.title: LoRA: a frozen matrix and a thin trainable detour
a35-lora.alt: A large hachured grey matrix W labelled frozen, holding 16.8 million parameters that never move, and beneath it a much thinner green path through two rank-eight matrices A and B holding 65,536 trainable parameters. Both paths meet at a sum node; the highlighted line underneath reads 0.39 percent trainable.

a37-hnsw.title: HNSW: hopping down the layers
a37-hnsw.alt: A three-layer navigable small-world graph. A query enters at the sparse top layer and follows numbered red hops greedily down through the denser layers to layer zero, where the nearest neighbour is ringed in green.

a41-prompt-injection.title: Prompt injection: an instruction that arrived as data
a41-prompt-injection.alt: A user question and a retrieved document chunk both cross a heavy red dashed trust boundary into one flat prompt string. The chunk contains a hidden instruction to email the thread to an attacker; the model obeys it and reaches a send_email tool, which is crossed out in red to mark where the breach actually happens.

p1-w05-m1.title: One HTTPS request is five round trips, and four are setup
p1-w05-m1.alt: A millisecond timeline of one HTTPS request drawn to scale: DNS to 6.9 ms, TCP handshake to 17.4, TLS to 32.3, server thinking to 45.2, and 221 KB of body arriving by 71.8 ms. A second row crosses out the three setup phases in red, and a third row shows the same request on a reused connection finishing in 39.5 ms. Bars below compare six fresh connections at 780 ms with six over one connection at 204 ms.

p1-w05-m2.title: Same pixels, two machine-readable outlines
p1-w05-m2.alt: One browser layout with header, nav, main, aside and footer produces two different trees: a crossed-out tree of nested divs that a screen reader announces as group, group, group, and a green tree of header, nav, main, article, aside and footer announced as banner, navigation, main, article, complementary, contentinfo. Below, a parser tape stalls for 120 ms at a blocking script, reaching domInteractive at 137.4 ms, against the same tape with defer reaching it at 2.4 ms.

p1-w05-m3.title: Flex distributes along one axis. Grid places into two.
p1-w05-m3.alt: The box model drawn as four nested rectangles from margin down to content, a specificity scoreboard scoring #nav .item a as 1-1-1 against a.item as 0-1-1 with !important crossed out, five flex cards wrapping along a single main axis beside a three-by-two grid whose container decides the placement, and a style-layout-paint-composite pipeline with measured layout times for 5000 items.

p1-w05-m4.title: The microtask queue is drained completely between every macrotask
p1-w05-m4.alt: A call stack holding the main script beside two trays: an upper microtask tray of promise callbacks and a lower macrotask tray of setTimeout and click. A green arrow runs from the microtask tray to the stack; a red arrow from the macrotask tray straight to the stack is crossed out because microtasks are still pending. Four numbered steps describe the cycle, and a strip of seven chips gives the verified output order from sync-start through to setTimeout zero last.

p1-w05-m5.title: One listener on the container. Four outcomes on every fetch.
p1-w05-m5.alt: A DOM tree from body down to three list items with the listener drawn on the ul, a dashed capture arrow going down the left and a solid bubble arrow coming back up the right, and a fourth dashed list item added later that is already handled. Beside it a two-by-two state box for loading, empty, error and success, and bars comparing ways of building 50 000 rows from innerHTML in a loop at roughly 309 seconds down to a virtualized 30 rows at 0.3 milliseconds.

p1-w06-m1.title: Nouns, verbs, and what OFFSET makes you read
p1-w06-m1.alt: A grid crossing two resources with GET, POST, PATCH and DELETE, filled with the status codes each returns, and an invented POST /getOrder cell crossed out in red. Beside it a single error envelope card with type, title, status, detail and errors. Below, offset pagination is drawn as 500 000 rows read and discarded in 693.9 ms against a keyset query that seeks straight to the same 20 rows in 1.7 milliseconds.

p1-w06-m2.title: One event loop per worker. Block it and everyone waits.
p1-w06-m2.alt: A request path from socket through uvicorn, Starlette and FastAPI to your handler, feeding a single event loop drawn as a circle inside a dashed worker-process boundary. Three branches leave the loop: an async handler that awaits and yields at 470 requests per second, an async handler containing a blocking call which is crossed out in red at 16.9 requests per second, and a plain def handler served by a forty-thread pool at 538. Bars at concurrency 200 compare 2565, 655 and 16.9 requests per second.

p1-w06-m3.title: Validation is a pipeline, and it collects every error in one pass
p1-w06-m3.alt: A JSON payload card with two bad fields feeding a four-gate vertical pipeline: before-validators on the raw input, type coercion and Field constraints, after-validators on the typed value, and finally the cross-field model validator. An arrow trying to skip from gate one to gate three is crossed out in red. On the right, a ValidationError card lists both errors with their type, loc and msg, and bars show model_validate at 2.70 microseconds against json.loads plus validate at 5.10.

p1-w06-m4.title: Three gates. Skipping the third one is called IDOR.
p1-w06-m4.alt: A request carrying a token passes through three gates: authentication answering who you are, route authorization answering whether your role may call this endpoint, and a thick green object-level gate answering whether row 4102 actually belongs to user 7. A red arrow going from the second gate straight to the database is crossed out and labelled IDOR. Bars compare argon2id hashing at 65.5 ms with bcrypt at cost 10, 12 and 14.

p1-w06-m5.title: Most tests need no network. Capacity is at the knee.
p1-w06-m5.alt: A test pyramid with a wide base of unit tests at about 1 ms each, a middle band of TestClient endpoint tests at about 50 ms each, and a narrow top of contract and smoke tests against a deployment. Beside it, a plot of offered concurrency against throughput and p99 latency: throughput rises then flattens while p99 climbs steeply, and the crossing point is ringed and labelled THE KNEE. The average-latency curve is crossed out as useless. Below, /healthz and /readyz are separated, with one shared handler crossed out.

p1-w07-m1.title: Each normal form removes one named anomaly
p1-w07-m1.alt: One wide table repeating the same customer and city on three order rows, with the city column ringed in red and one value misspelled to show the update anomaly. Three numbered steps below name what each normal form removes, and the result is drawn as three tables — customers, orders and order_items — linked by hand-drawn foreign key arrows, beside a green box showing a deliberate denormalization and its write cost.

p1-w07-m2.title: The FK lives on the many side
p1-w07-m2.alt: Customers linked one-to-many to orders with the crow's foot and the foreign key drawn on the orders side. Below, a direct many-to-many link between orders and products is crossed out in red because there is nowhere to put the key, and redrawn with an order_items junction table holding the composite primary key plus quantity and unit price. Three side boxes give the rules for money, time and status columns.

p1-w07-m3.title: A join is row multiplication, not a Venn diagram
p1-w07-m3.alt: Three order rows linked to seven order-item rows, producing a joined result of seven rows in which each order's total is repeated once per item; the repeated totals are ringed in red. A Venn diagram is crossed out because it cannot show duplicates. Two SUM boxes show the correct 507,507,500 against the join-inflated 1,522,492,500, a 3.0x difference with no error raised. Below, INNER, LEFT, RIGHT and FULL joins are drawn as result rows with NULL ghosts.

p1-w07-m4.title: GROUP BY throws the rows away. A window keeps them.
p1-w07-m4.alt: Eight input rows collapsed by GROUP BY into three, beside the same eight rows kept intact with a running-total column added, dashed PARTITION BY dividers between categories and a bracket marking the sliding frame. Below, sum(x) over the tied input 1,1,2,3,3,4 with a 1 PRECEDING frame gives 1,2,3,5,6,7 under ROWS and 2,2,4,8,8,10 under RANGE, with the tied pairs ringed in red.

p1-w07-m5.title: An UPDATE writes a new row version and keeps the old one
p1-w07-m5.alt: A PostgreSQL heap drawn as page rectangles: two pages of live tuples at 48 MB, then twelve pages after five rounds of full-table updates, ten of them dead, at 284 MB for the same 200 000 live rows. VACUUM marks the dead pages free but the file stays 284 MB; VACUUM FULL rewrites the heap back down to 47 MB at the cost of an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.

p1-w08-m1.title: The log is flushed first. That is why "none" survives a power cut.
p1-w08-m1.alt: A transaction box with BEGIN at the top and COMMIT at the bottom containing a debit of 50 000 and a matching credit, struck by a red lightning bolt labelled kill -9. The balances before and after the crash are identical at 100 000 each. Below, a numbered pair of steps shows the write-ahead log record being fsynced first and the data pages written later, with the reversed order crossed out in red.

p1-w08-m2.title: Both sessions read 10 before either wrote. One sale vanished.
p1-w08-m2.alt: Two session timelines under READ COMMITTED: A begins and reads stock 10, B reads 10 as well, then both write 9 and both commit, so the final stock is 9 after two sales — the overlap where both reads happen is boxed in red. Below, the same two sessions with SELECT FOR UPDATE: B stalls as a dashed waiting bar until A commits, then reads 9 and writes 8. A ladder of isolation levels and measured throughput on one hot row complete the picture.

p1-w08-m3.title: Read every page, or follow three pointers
p1-w08-m3.alt: On the left, a sequential scan drawn as seventy-two heap pages all swept, removing 333,332 rows per worker in 86.8 milliseconds. On the right, a B-tree with the descent path from root through one internal node to one leaf traced in bold with numbered steps, reaching the row in 0.033 milliseconds, with 1970x written between them. Below, a composite index on (customer_id, placed_at) is drawn as sorted keys grouped by customer, serving a leftmost-prefix query in 0.512 ms while a second-column-only predicate falls back to a 116.6 ms scan.

p1-w08-m4.title: One loop, five hundred round trips
p1-w08-m4.alt: A Python loop firing eight drawn arrows and an implied five hundred separate SELECTs at a database, crossed out in red, at 501 queries and 1321.5 milliseconds; beside it the same loop with selectinload issuing two fat arrows at 61.6 milliseconds. Below, the SQLAlchemy Session is drawn as an identity map plus a pending-changes list, flushed in order at commit, with bars comparing ORM add_all at 5448 ms against COPY at 518 ms for 100 000 rows.

p1-w08-m5.title: A cold key turns 40 readers into 40 identical queries
p1-w08-m5.alt: A three-layer stack with the repository Protocol marked as the swap point tests replace. Below, forty concurrent readers all miss a cold cache and all reach the database — forty calls in 1784 milliseconds, with the fan of arrows crossed out — against the same readers funnelled through a single-flight loader into one database call in 85 milliseconds. A timeline at the bottom shades the stale window between the write and the TTL expiry.

p2-w09-m1.title: Everything, out of one part
p2-w09-m1.alt: A whiteboard sketch: a single NAND gate and its four-row truth table, then NOT built by tying a NAND's two inputs together, AND built from two NANDs, OR built from three NANDs by De Morgan and XOR wired out in full from four NANDs, each panel labelled with its gate count and circuit depth, beside a price list of NAND counts and depths for six gates, with a five-gate AND/OR/NOT version of XOR crossed out in red.

p2-w09-m2.title: The carry is a chain, and the chain is the clock
p2-w09-m2.alt: A whiteboard sketch building a half adder from an XOR and an AND gate, then a full adder from two half adders and an OR gate, then four full adders wired in a row computing 0111 plus 0001 with the carry drawn as thick red arrows travelling right to left through every stage, and a bar chart comparing ripple-carry gate depth of 19 to 259 against Kogge-Stone depth of 12 to 28 for adders four to sixty-four bits wide.

p2-w09-m3.title: One adder, six switches, eighteen operations
p2-w09-m3.alt: A whiteboard sketch of the Hack ALU: two sixteen-wire buses x and y pass through four amber control switches zx, nx, zy and ny into a single block that computes both x plus y and x and y, a multiplexer selects between them under control bit f, an output switch no can invert the result, and two status wires zr and ng peel off the output bus; beneath it a control table with six of the eighteen documented bit patterns and the subtraction row highlighted, a worked trace of three minus five, and a rejected design of eighteen separate circuits crossed out in red.

p2-w09-m4.title: A loop of wire, a clock edge, and the wall behind them
p2-w09-m4.alt: A whiteboard sketch building memory in four steps - two inverters wired in a loop that holds a bit, the same loop plus a clock making a D flip-flop with the rising edge marked as the only instant anything changes, a multiplexer added so a load line chooses between keeping and replacing, and sixteen of those making a register with eight registers plus an address making a RAM - beside a log-scaled bar chart of the memory hierarchy from a one-nanosecond L1 hit to a hundred-microsecond NVMe read, and an eight-by-eight grid showing one cache line fully used when sweeping along a row and almost entirely wasted when jumping down a column.

p2-w09-m5.title: An instruction is just wires
p2-w09-m5.alt: A whiteboard sketch of a sixteen-bit Hack C-instruction drawn as sixteen labelled bit boxes with brackets peeling off each field to what it drives - the opcode, the a bit, the six ALU control pins, the three destination bits and the three jump bits - beside the fetch, decode, execute and write-back loop drawn around a central program counter, a hand-ruled trace table of a six-instruction program showing A, D, M and the PC after each step, a staircase pipeline diagram with one mispredicted branch crossed out in red, and a four-lane SIMD panel annotated with a measured 4.79 times speedup.

p2-w10-m1.title: Five envelopes, five questions
p2-w10-m1.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing a packet as five nested rectangles labelled Ethernet, IP, TCP, TLS and HTTP wrapped around a scrap of JSON, with the single question each layer answers written beside it and the header sizes of 14, 20 and 20 bytes noted, next to a measured timeline of one real HTTPS request broken into 4 millisecond DNS, 22.6 millisecond TCP, 32.5 millisecond TLS and 29.6 millisecond request segments totalling 88.7 milliseconds, the same timeline again with the first three segments crossed out under keep-alive, and a seven-hop traceroute reaching a CDN edge in 20.3 milliseconds.

p2-w10-m2.title: TCP buys reliability with round trips
p2-w10-m2.alt: A whiteboard sketch with client and server timelines and the three-way handshake drawn as crossing arrows labelled SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK with a circled measured cost of 22.6 milliseconds, then four data segments where the second is crossed out in red mid-flight, a duplicate acknowledgement returns and the segment is retransmitted in green while everything behind it stalls; a bandwidth-delay-product pipe worked out as 1.22 megabytes in flight; and two lower panels showing a thousand small TCP sends coalescing into 413 differently sized reads against UDP datagrams drawn as sealed envelopes that keep their boundaries but two of which are crossed out as lost.

p2-w10-m3.title: The lifecycle is fixed. The shape is your choice.
p2-w10-m3.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing the socket lifecycle as a ladder of server calls socket, bind, listen and accept beside the client's socket and connect, with the three-way handshake marked as happening inside connect and accept returning a brand new socket; a byte stream drawn as alternating four-byte length tags and messages with red cut marks at every boundary and a crossed-out claim that one recv equals one message; and three panels comparing a thread-per-connection server at 1002 threads and 35.7 KiB per connection, a select loop at 2 threads and 0.9 KiB, and asyncio at 2 threads and 6.0 KiB, with measured p99 latencies of 180.7, 79.7 and 266.7 microseconds.

p2-w10-m4.title: Framing, encoding, semantics - and the peer you did not upgrade
p2-w10-m4.alt: A whiteboard sketch dividing a protocol into three separated bands labelled framing, encoding and semantics, each with the single question it answers; the same message drawn to scale as bars of 113.8 bytes of JSON, 81.1 bytes of MessagePack and 47.8 bytes of Protobuf with measured decode times of 4.44, 1.19 and 1.84 microseconds beneath; a compatibility panel where an old v1 client silently ignores a new currency field but a renamed field is crossed out in red; and a reconnect timeline with retries at one, two, four and eight seconds plus jitter, above a struck-through row of evenly spaced retries labelled thundering herd.

p2-w10-m5.title: Encrypted is not the same as safe
p2-w10-m5.alt: A whiteboard sketch contrasting a properly authenticated TLS connection, drawn as a locked tube between client and server carrying confidentiality, integrity and authentication, with the same picture under verify=False where an attacker is spliced into the middle holding two perfectly good tunnels and the client's lock is crossed out in red; below it the chain of trust from root CA to intermediate to leaf with a self-signed certificate crossed out, a to-scale comparison of a 53 millisecond TLS 1.2 handshake against a 32.5 millisecond TLS 1.3 handshake and a zero-RTT stub marked replayable, and a reverse proxy box annotated with the three things it changes.

p2-w11-m1.title: A point, an arrow, and an angle
p2-w11-m1.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing the vector (3,4) drawn both as a red dot and as a blue arrow from the origin with its 3-4-5 right triangle and the norm worked out as five; two arrows u and v with the angle between them marked and the dot product formula written out with cosine theta circled; three document vectors showing that a short and a long document about cats point the same way while a tax-law document is ninety degrees away, with the Euclidean distance between the two cat documents struck through in red; a unit circle with the same arrows normalised onto it; and two histograms of pairwise distances that are wide at two dimensions and collapse to a thin spike at a thousand.

p2-w11-m2.title: A matrix is a picture of what it does
p2-w11-m2.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing four unit squares transformed by a scale, a shear, a forty-five degree rotation and a rank-deficient squash that collapses the square onto a single red line, each with the image of the basis vectors drawn as a blue and a green arrow and the determinant written beneath; the determinant shown as the area of the transformed square going from one to four to zero; the three equivalent readings of a matrix product listed with numbered badges; a shape-check ladder where the inner dimensions of a batched matmul are ringed and joined; and a log-scaled bar chart of matmul throughput from 0.013 GFLOP per second for naive Python loops to 1550 for single-precision BLAS.

p2-w11-m3.title: Keep the big stretches, throw the rest away
p2-w11-m3.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing a dashed unit circle deformed into a tilted ellipse with the two eigenvector directions drawn as bold red arrows labelled with stretch factors of 3.1 and 0.6; the singular value decomposition drawn as a chain of four shapes - circle, rotated circle, stretched ellipse and rotated ellipse - with the arrows between them labelled V transpose, sigma and U and the semi-axes marked sigma one and sigma two; a strip of one photograph rebuilt at ranks 1, 5, 20 and 50 with the fraction of energy kept written under each and rank 20 picked out as 98.1 percent of the matrix for 12.8 times fewer numbers; a scree plot with the elbow marked; and the LoRA picture of a frozen 4096-by-4096 weight matrix beside two thin adapters holding 131,072 parameters instead of 16,777,216.

p2-w11-m4.title: The nudges multiply
p2-w11-m4.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing a curve with a red secant line through two points a distance h apart converging to a green tangent as h shrinks; a contour map with a red arrow pointing straight uphill perpendicular to the contour and a green arrow pointing the opposite way; a chain of three function boxes f, g and h with blue forward arrows carrying values left to right and red backward arrows carrying local derivatives right to left, with the product dL/dx equals dL/db times db/da times da/dx written beneath; a comparison of forward mode needing n separate passes against reverse mode needing one backward sweep; and a U-shaped plot of finite-difference error against step size with the optimum marked at h equals one times ten to the minus four.

p2-w11-m5.title: The learning rate has a hard ceiling
p2-w11-m5.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing the same parabola four times with a ball descending it - crawling when the learning rate is far below two over L, landing in a few steps near one over L, bouncing between two points forever at exactly two over L, and flying apart above it with that panel crossed out in red - with the stability condition lr less than two over L circled; a contour map of a narrow Rosenbrock valley where plain gradient descent zig-zags across the walls in red while Adam walks down the floor in green; a results table showing gradient descent, momentum, Nesterov and RMSProp never reaching a loss below one thousandth in five thousand steps while Adam does at step 3051; and a stacked bar chart of the 107.84 gigabytes a seven-billion-parameter full fine-tune needs beside a 3.50 gigabyte QLoRA bar.

p2-w12-m1.title: A 99% accurate test that is wrong 92% of the time
p2-w12-m1.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing ten thousand people as one long rectangle with a tiny red sliver of ten actual cases, brackets leading down to a small green bar of nine true positives beside a red bar drawn ten times longer holding 101 false positives, with the precision worked out as eight percent; a curve of precision collapsing from 0.985 at 13.4 percent prevalence to 0.040 at 0.01 percent on a real spam classifier whose sensitivity and specificity never changed; the odds form of Bayes' theorem worked through to one in twenty-four; and the claim that a model is ninety-nine percent accurate crossed out in red.

p2-w12-m2.title: The mean describes almost nobody
p2-w12-m2.alt: A whiteboard sketch of twenty thousand real HTTP latencies drawn as a histogram with a sharp peak at 0.165 milliseconds and a long thin red tail out to 6.876 milliseconds, with dashed lines marking p50, the mean at 0.191, p95, p99 and the maximum, annotated that only 19.8 percent of requests are slower than the mean and that the skewness is 20.56; an SLA on average latency crossed out in red beside an SLA on p99 ticked; four small histograms of sample means at n equal to 1, 5, 30 and 1000 whose skewness falls from 12.90 to 0.62 as the shape becomes symmetric; and a QQ plot whose points bend up away from the diagonal at the right.

p2-w12-m3.title: Interval the difference, not the two numbers
p2-w12-m3.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing a population cloud with a sample scooped from it and an inference arrow back; the bootstrap drawn as four resampled rows with the duplicated values marked in red feeding a histogram whose 2.5 and 97.5 percent cut points are dashed in; two model confidence intervals for F1 of 0.9231 and 0.9518 drawn as overlapping bars with the conclusion that they are not significantly different crossed out; the paired difference interval of plus 0.0287 with bounds 0.0074 to 0.0538 drawn entirely to the right of zero and P of B better than A at 99.66 percent; and a struck-through list of the three things a p-value is not.

p2-w12-m4.title: Randomisation is the whole argument
p2-w12-m4.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing a stream of users passing through a coin-flip splitter into arms A and B, with arm B crossed out in red because a sample ratio mismatch of 50,000 against 48,000 gives chi-squared 40.82 and p equal to 1.7 times ten to the minus ten; a bar chart of required sample size rising from 8,158 per arm for a twenty percent lift to 122,124 for a five percent lift; a wandering p-value line crossing the 0.05 threshold several times with the first crossing ringed in red and false-positive rates of 5.1, 8.2, 13.6, 18.8 and 25.1 percent for one, two, five, ten and twenty looks; two scatter clouds showing CUPED tightening the variance by 81 percent; and a blank pre-registration card.

p2-w12-m5.title: Every subgroup can disagree with the total
p2-w12-m5.alt: A whiteboard sketch of the 1973 Berkeley admissions data drawn as six departments, each showing a blue dot for men and a green dot for women with women equal or higher in four of six, arranged along a steep red downward trend line so the aggregate reads men 44.5 percent against women 30.4 percent; three small causal diagrams distinguishing a confounder, a collider and a mediator with what to control for written under each; two scatter plots where a single outlier takes the Pearson correlation from 0.895 to 0.087 while Spearman stays at 0.885; and a bar showing 257 of 4,950 pairs of pure noise variables reaching p below 0.05.

p2-w13-m1.title: Big-O is a shape, not a speed
p2-w13-m1.alt: A whiteboard sketch with four labelled growth curves for constant, logarithmic, linear and quadratic work; two lines of identical linear complexity measured a million elements apart, one an array walk at 32.6 milliseconds and one a shuffled linked-list walk at 661 milliseconds with a 20.3 times gap arrowed between them; a crossover plot where an n-squared curve sits below an n-log-n curve until about forty elements, with the advice to always pick the lower Big-O crossed out in red; and nine groups of three tally marks illustrating the accounting argument that makes a doubling array's append amortized constant time.

p2-w13-m2.title: The window remembers
p2-w13-m2.alt: A whiteboard sketch of a twelve-cell array where the naive approach of recomputing every window of four is struck through in red and labelled n windows times k work; the same array with left and right pointer arrows under a highlighted window and a running sum of 14; the window advanced one cell with a green plus-arr-of-R arrow entering and a red minus-arr-of-L arrow leaving to give 15 in two operations; both pointers shown traversing the array exactly once for linear total work; and a prefix-sum row beneath the array with the formula P of j plus one minus P of i, annotated with measured timings of 503.8 milliseconds naive against 2.16 milliseconds with prefix sums.

p2-w13-m3.title: Two data structures, wired together
p2-w13-m3.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing a hash map of four keys each pointing at a node, labelled as answering where but not when; the same four nodes drawn as a doubly linked list from head to tail labelled as answering when but not where, with a singly linked version crossed out; then both wired together for a get of key C, with numbered strokes following the map pointer to the node, unlinking it by joining its two neighbours and splicing it in at the head in three pointer writes; and an eviction where the tail node is crossed out of both the list and the map, annotated with measured costs of 211 nanoseconds per operation and an 84.4 percent hit rate.

p2-w13-m4.title: A hash table keeps empty space on purpose
p2-w13-m4.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing four hash buckets with the keys ann, bob and cy hashed and masked into them and the arithmetic written out; a fourth key dee colliding and being hung off a bucket as a chain at 1.15 probes; the same collision resolved by open addressing with numbered probes walking right two occupied slots before landing in a free one; a resize where the four-bucket table is crossed out in red and every key is redrawn into an eight-bucket table because the mask changed; and a plot of average probes against load factor where chaining stays nearly flat from 1.15 to 1.50 while open addressing climbs from 1.22 to 40.99, with a worst observed probe count of 15,832.

p2-w13-m5.title: You never needed the stream. You needed 100 slots.
p2-w13-m5.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing a stream of ten million values flowing off the page with the naive approach of collecting and sorting everything crossed out in red at 22.37 seconds and 411.6 megabytes; a six-node min-heap with the root ringed and labelled the bouncer; the two-way decision where a value greater than the root replaces it and sifts down in about seven swaps while a smaller value is discarded after one comparison; a sift-down drawn with numbered swaps; and a bar chart where the bounded heap uses 14.8 megabytes against 411.6, at 2.00 seconds against 22.37.

p2-w14-m1.title: O(log n) is a promise about a BALANCED tree
p2-w14-m1.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing seven values inserted in shuffled order forming a neat binary search tree of depth three, beside the same seven values inserted in ascending order forming a diagonal chain of depth seven with the word tree crossed out and replaced by linked list; measured bars showing depth 41 and 21.4 comparisons per lookup for shuffled insertion against depth 100,000 and 50,419 comparisons for sorted insertion, a factor of 2,356; and a B-Tree node drawn as a wide rectangle of about four hundred keys in one four-kilobyte page fanning out to three more, reaching a hundred million rows in three levels where a binary search tree needs twenty-seven.

p2-w14-m2.title: Index arithmetic IS the tree
p2-w14-m2.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing seven values drawn once as a binary tree and once as a flat array of seven boxes with indices zero to six, dotted lines connecting each tree node to its array slot, and the index arithmetic left equals 2i plus 1, right equals 2i plus 2, parent equals i minus 1 over 2 written beside it, with explicit parent and child pointer fields crossed out in red; a level-by-level accounting showing that half the nodes are leaves needing zero swaps while only the root needs log n, summing to linear work; a sift-down swapping down past the smaller child; and measured bars of 22.7 milliseconds for bottom-up heapify against 42.0 milliseconds for a million successive pushes.

p2-w14-m3.title: One word: queue or stack
p2-w14-m3.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing the same seven-node graph twice, once visited in breadth-first level order with dashed level rings and the word QUEUE circled, once visited in depth-first order with the word STACK circled, and the two nearly identical code fragments differing only in popleft versus pop; a topological sort peeling zero-in-degree nodes off a five-node directed graph with in-degrees written under each; the same graph with one red back edge added leaving three nodes whose in-degree never reaches zero, ringed in red as the cycle; and a memory comparison of 52.3 megabytes for an adjacency list against 1,250 megabytes for a bitset adjacency matrix.

p2-w14-m4.title: One number turns a circle into a beam
p2-w14-m4.alt: A whiteboard sketch contrasting Dijkstra's search, drawn as concentric red circles spreading in every direction from the start and past the goal after expanding 1,177,499 cells, with A star's search drawn as an ellipse stretched toward the goal expanding 792,399 cells, 1.49 times fewer; the formula f of n equals g of n plus h of n highlighted with g annotated as the known cost so far and h as a guess that must not overestimate, ringed in red; and a three-node counterexample where Dijkstra finalises node B at cost one before discovering a minus-ten edge that makes the true cost minus five, with the earlier decision struck through.

p2-w14-m5.title: It is not the recursion. It is the repetition.
p2-w14-m5.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing the full fib(5) recursion tree with every occurrence of fib(2) ringed in red and fib(3) in amber, annotated with 29,860,703 naive calls for fib(35); the same tree with the repeated subtrees struck out and a memo table being filled, annotated with 69 calls and a 432,764 times reduction; an edit-distance grid between kitten and sitting with one cell highlighted and three arrows entering it from above, from the left and from the diagonal labelled delete, insert and substitute; and a memory comparison of a 634.67 megabyte full matrix struck through against 0.33 megabytes for two rows, with the warning that two rows cannot reconstruct the alignment path.

p2-w15-m1.title: Row storage makes you read everything
p2-w15-m1.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing a CSV drawn as seven rows of eight shaded cells where seven of every eight cells are struck through as wasted, annotated that a sum over one column still reads all 663.3 megabytes; Parquet drawn as eight vertical strips whose widths are the real compressed column sizes from 69.5 megabytes for the timestamp down to 0.5 for a boolean, with only the 20.9 megabyte amount strip shaded; the same file split into ten row groups where nine are struck through in red because the footer statistics proved they cannot contain matching rows; and measured bars showing count star at 0.43 seconds on CSV against 0.0019 on Parquet, and sum of amount at 0.78 against 0.047.

p2-w15-m2.title: The rows and the cursor commit together, or not at all
p2-w15-m2.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing three pagination styles with offset pagination crossed out in red because rows shift between pages; an exponential backoff timeline with marks at one, two, four and eight seconds plus dashed jitter marks; the central idea drawn as one green box containing both the thousand fetched rows and the cursor value 43000 with a single commit arrow leaving it, and the two alternative orderings struck through as causing duplicates or data loss; and a progress bar to a hundred thousand records with a crash marked at forty-three thousand, annotated that resuming took exactly one hundred API calls in total, the same as an uninterrupted run, with matching checksums.

p2-w15-m3.title: A scraper does not throw. It returns None.
p2-w15-m3.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing a web page with a price cell highlighted beside two selectors - a brittle chain of positional child selectors and a generated class name struck through in red, and a resilient selector anchored to the Price label ticked in green; the central failure mode where a missing element returns None rather than raising and fills a warehouse column with NULLs with no exception and no log line; the fix as one guard line that raises at the extraction boundary so a CI job goes red on the pull request; and measured parse times of 2.72 seconds for BeautifulSoup with html.parser, 2.25 with lxml, and 0.159 seconds for direct lxml XPath.

p2-w15-m4.title: The default is to absorb the surprise
p2-w15-m4.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing three upstream schema changes and dlt's default handling of each - a new currency field becoming a column with nulls backfilled, a quoted string amount silently coerced to a double, and a removed field leaving the column with a null - then a four-position schema contract knob where evolve adds the column and loads the row, freeze raises a DataValidationError and loads nothing, discard_value loads the row without the column and discard_row makes the row vanish silently, with discard_row ringed in red; a nested JSON blob normalized into an orders table and an orders__items child table joined by generated id columns; and the actual freeze error message.

p2-w15-m5.title: DuckDB never materialised the rows
p2-w15-m5.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing a star schema with a narrow ten-million-row fact table at the centre and four small dimension tables around it; a slowly-changing dimension drawn as three stacked versions of one merchant row carrying valid-from, valid-to and is-current, with an as-of query landing on the middle row; a bar chart of one group-by over ten million rows where DuckDB takes 0.117 seconds and 96 megabytes against pandas at 1.510 seconds and 878 megabytes, with polars in between; and two directory trees where daily partitions are marked good and two hundred and fifty thousand per-user directories are crossed out in red.

p2-w16-m1.title: One flat block, plus a rule for walking it
p2-w16-m1.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing twelve values as one contiguous strip of memory with a three-by-four grid drawn above it and dotted lines connecting a few grid cells to their positions in the strip, annotated shape (3,4) strides (32,8); a transpose that changes only the strides in a quarter of a microsecond against np.ascontiguousarray copying 128 megabytes in 43.6 milliseconds; three ways of selecting every other element of a 400 megabyte array where slicing is a free view at 1.46 microseconds while fancy indexing at 70.1 milliseconds and boolean masking at 116.1 milliseconds each copy 200 megabytes; the broadcasting rule aligning shapes from the right with a mismatched case crossed out; and measured row and column traversal times differing sevenfold with memory order.

p2-w16-m2.title: One duplicated key and the total is wrong
p2-w16-m2.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing a left table of three orders joined to a right table whose key A appears twice, ringed in red, so the result has four rows and the amount for A is counted twice, making a sum of 700 instead of 600 with no error; the fix of passing validate equals m colon 1 raising a MergeError instead; a bar chart of where a five-million-row DataFrame's 404.4 megabytes go, dominated by a 279.4 megabyte object column that becomes 5.0 megabytes as a category; and per-row costs of 112 nanoseconds for Series.apply against 0.4 nanoseconds vectorized, with iterrows at 9.33 microseconds per row struck through.

p2-w16-m3.title: Leak size is a number you can measure
p2-w16-m3.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing the folklore that fitting an imputer across the train-test split inflates scores crossed out in red beside the measured result of minus 0.007 to minus 0.0004 AUC, that is no inflation; a horizontal scale from zero to plus 0.4 with measured leak sizes marked - about zero for mean, KNN and iterative imputation, plus 0.148 for duplicated rows, plus 0.275 for target encoding on pure noise and plus 0.356 for feature selection over twenty thousand features; the rule that leak size scales with how much the transform uses the target times how many candidates it searched, worked through three examples; a plot of inflation rising from 0.184 to 0.356 as the number of searched features grows on pure noise; and a sklearn Pipeline drawn inside the cross-validation fold boundary.

p2-w16-m4.title: Plot it first. Then bring an effect size.
p2-w16-m4.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing a clearly parabolic scatter plot annotated with a Pearson correlation of minus 0.02 ringed in red and labelled blind while mutual information reads 0.98, and a sine-wave scatter with correlation plus 0.24 against mutual information 0.91; a table showing a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test flagging a shift of one hundredth of a standard deviation zero percent of the time at a thousand samples and a hundred percent of the time at a million; a two-gate design requiring both a p-value below 0.01 and a KS statistic above 0.1; and a numbered six-step EDA checklist.

p2-w16-m5.title: A chart is an argument
p2-w16-m5.alt: A whiteboard sketch showing three nearly identical accuracy values of 95.1, 95.4 and 95.7 drawn as bars on an axis starting at 95.0 so they appear seven times different, beside the same values drawn from zero where the bars are indistinguishable; a line chart with a truncated axis marked as legitimate because a change from a baseline is the point, with the rule that bars encode length and must start at zero while lines encode position and need not; the same ten million points drawn as an unreadable solid scatter blob against a hexbin at 0.66 seconds and a two-dimensional histogram at 1.05 seconds, both showing clear density structure; and a red-green line chart rendered as indistinguishable greys under a colour-blindness simulation beside the fix using different line styles and direct labels.

p3-w17-m1.title: Training is a search, judged behind a wall
p3-w17-m1.alt: A small feature table whose price column is separated in green feeds a dashed cloud of candidate lines through six scatter points; three candidates are dashed red with crosses and one is solid green, while on the right a dashed padlocked wall separates train and validation blocks from a locked twenty-percent test block, an arrow from test back to the cloud is struck out and labelled peeking, and two bars compare a baseline mean absolute error of 0.906 with the model's 0.533.

p3-w17-m2.title: The gradient is an average of error times feature
p3-w17-m2.alt: Three hand-drawn panels: eight points with red vertical residual segments dropping onto a fitted line, the mean-squared-error gradient derived in three badged steps ending in the highlighted phrase average of error times feature, and two contour plots contrasting a near-circular scaled loss surface where four green arrows walk to the minimum with a long thin unscaled ravine at condition number 5.642e10 where a red zig-zag path diverges.

p3-w17-m3.title: The curve is the model; the threshold is a business decision
p3-w17-m3.alt: A logistic S-curve drawn through eighteen pass and fail study-hour points, with a red dashed vertical threshold at 2.710 hours carrying a slider handle and a double-headed arrow, beside two insets contrasting the clean log-loss bowl with a crossed-out flat-shelved squared-error curve at curvature -0.120, and two arrows of wildly different length showing a 203-times gradient difference on the same wrong point.

p3-w17-m4.title: The U-curve does not end where the textbook stops drawing
p3-w17-m4.alt: Bias falling and variance rising combine into a thick U-shaped total test-error curve that spikes to a test MSE of 17.8 at the interpolation threshold and then descends a second time to 0.0569, all sitting above a dashed irreducible noise floor of 0.0625, with three small polynomial fits below of which the degree-fifteen snake is crossed out at coefficient norm 6342, and an L2 circle touched mid-arc beside an L1 diamond touched exactly at its corner.

p3-w17-m5.title: The Pipeline makes leakage impossible, not merely discouraged
p3-w17-m5.alt: A wrong workflow at the top where a scaler and selector are fitted on all data before the five cross-validation folds, crossed out in red and annotated 0.815 accuracy on pure noise, above a correct workflow where each fold carries its own fit step and scores 0.510, with the 30.5-point gap circled between them, and the Pipeline object drawn on the right as a ColumnTransformer feeding a LogisticRegression under a single fit arrow.

p3-w18-m1.title: A tree can only cut along the axes
p3-w18-m1.alt: Two scatter panels: on the left a diagonal class boundary approximated by an eight-step blue staircase of axis-aligned cuts, on the right the same points with the axes rotated so a single green vertical cut separates them, with depth-three tree accuracy rising from 0.9105 to 1.0000, above the Gini arithmetic for one split ending in a circled gain of 0.1250, a three-level tree whose leaves carry class counts, and two near-identical datasets differing by one flipped label growing visibly different trees.

p3-w18-m2.title: A forest only helps as far as the trees disagree
p3-w18-m2.alt: Ten training rows resampled into three bootstrap bags where about a third of rows in each bag are drawn dashed and marked out-of-bag and others are marked drawn twice, feeding three visibly different trees into a circled AVERAGE, beside a table of max_features against tree correlation 0.53 to 0.68 and accuracy, the variance formula with the correlation term circled in red, and two importance bar charts where a pure-noise customer_id column takes 0.8182 of the in-sample impurity credit and zero of the held-out permutation credit.

p3-w18-m3.title: Each tree is fitted to what is still wrong
p3-w18-m3.alt: Four panels showing the same eight points fitted by a step function that gains one step per boosting stage, with the red vertical residual bars visibly shrinking and the sum of squared errors falling from 163.88 to 41.87 to 16.24 to 11.11, beneath which the Newton leaf-weight formula is written out with the curvature term circled and three lambda values shrinking the leaf from -0.286 to -0.019, and a bar chart where max_depth at 0.0101 dwarfs learning_rate at 0.0006.

p3-w18-m4.title: Two trivial steps, and one hidden assumption
p3-w18-m4.alt: Twelve points assigned to three cross-marked centres with dashed Voronoi boundaries, then the same points with the centres arrowed to their group means and ghosts left where they were, looped back by a curved repeat arrow annotated inertia 1200.2 to 566.9, beside three crossed-out failure panels for moon-shaped, anisotropic and unequal-variance data with adjusted Rand scores of 0.2549, 0.8995 and 0.8265 and their density- or mixture-model fixes, and a bottom pair showing the worse silhouette belongs to the better clustering.

p3-w18-m5.title: t-SNE and UMAP destroy size and distance on purpose
p3-w18-m5.alt: Four panels comparing a twenty-dimensional truth of two small close clusters and one four-times-wider cluster 6.63 times further away, a PCA projection that preserves both ratios, and crossed-out t-SNE and UMAP projections that equalise the cluster sizes and, for UMAP, reverse the ordering, beside three struck-through claims the picture cannot support and a bottom strip where fifty-dimensional pure noise projects into three convincing blobs at silhouette 0.3461.

p3-w19-m1.title: Four cells, and every metric is a ratio of them
p3-w19-m1.alt: A two-by-two confusion matrix with TN 11, FP 3, FN 2 and TP 4, with a yellow highlighter swipe along the bottom row for recall (4 over 6) and down the right column for precision (4 over 7), beside a struck-out first attempt with the axes swapped; below, three bar pairs at falling fraud prevalence where ROC-AUC stays flat near 0.96 while precision at ninety percent recall collapses from 0.8418 to 0.0110; and at the foot a measured precision-recall curve with three operating points marked on it - the 0.5 default at recall 0.60 costing GBP 22,480, the F1-maximising 0.0693 at recall 0.77 costing GBP 13,080, and the cost-optimal 0.0221 at recall 0.82 costing GBP 10,180 - falling off a cliff to 0.011 precision at 0.90 recall.

p3-w19-m2.title: A metric is a claim about which errors you will trade
p3-w19-m2.alt: Three loss shapes drawn over one error axis - a V for absolute error targeting the median, a parabola for squared error targeting the mean, and a tilted pinball V targeting the ninetieth percentile - with MAPE struck out beside them, two ranked lists of ten whose identical recall at five hides an MRR of 0.50 against 1.00, and a reliability diagram where a raw booster's curve sags well below the diagonal at ECE 0.1366 until Platt scaling pulls it back to 0.0188.

p3-w19-m3.title: The split has to mirror how the model gets used
p3-w19-m3.alt: Four split strategies drawn as bars: a single hold-out at sd 0.0116, five folds at sd 0.0032, a grouped bar of eight customers with a red cut struck out where a random split slices through one customer's rows costing four points of lie, and a time-series staircase with a crossed-out backward arrow that trains on the future for fifteen AUC points, beside a nested cross-validation sketch and an adversarial-validation scatter scoring AUC 0.7902 against a 0.5070 control.

p3-w19-m4.title: Nine ways information crosses the wall
p3-w19-m4.alt: A padlocked dashed wall divides a TRAIN block from the test side, crossed by nine red arrows whose thickness is proportional to the measured inflation each kind of leakage produces, from 33.50 points for feature selection on all labels down to 2.28 for duplicate rows, with a green Pipeline box below noted as blocking five of the nine by construction and a shuffled-label test whose 0.72 bar is crossed out against the 0.50 it should have produced.

p3-w19-m5.title: One number hides the slice where it fails
p3-w19-m5.alt: A staircase of baseline scores climbing from random 0.4997 through one feature 0.8014 to the model 0.8991, beside a confident overall accuracy bar cracking into a strong self-serve slice at 0.9548 and a weak enterprise slice at 0.5842 whose boxes are redrawn proportional to revenue rather than row count, giving a revenue-weighted 0.8457, plus two bootstrap confidence intervals drawn against a heavy zero line and a three-box offline-shadow-online chain with two boxes still empty.

p3-w20-m1.title: The encoder is a property of the model
p3-w20-m1.alt: Three columns: paired raw and scaled accuracy bars showing KNN gaining 35.9 points and a boosted tree gaining nothing from standardising, a forty-level category fanning into one-hot, ordinal and target encodings with logistic regression gaining 9.77 AUC points from one-hot while HistGB gains 0.23, and three target-encoding schemes of which the 0.7471 full-dataset version and the 0.6234 reused-fold version are struck out leaving out-of-fold at 0.6423.

p3-w20-m2.title: An aggregate 'as of today' is a different feature
p3-w20-m2.alt: A customer's transaction timeline cut by a red dashed prediction moment, with a red bracket spanning the whole history struck out beyond that moment and a green bracket stopping at it, above a ledger showing the leaky feature's reported cross-validated AUC of 0.8421, the 0.8076 production actually delivered and the 0.8303 an honest model would have given, plus a clock showing hours 23 and 0 one step apart against a number line where they sit 23 apart, and three text representations sized by artifact.

p3-w20-m3.title: Cutting features is free until the cliff
p3-w20-m3.alt: A test-AUC curve staying flat at 0.979 from two hundred features down to fifty, dipping to 0.97051 at twenty-five and then falling off a red cliff through 0.95181 and 0.90541 to 0.80608 at five features, with the flat part highlighted; below, a crossed-out pair of inference-latency bars showing 1.47 against 1.83 microseconds per row, and a grid of two hundred column squares shrinking to twenty-five with the other 175 swept into a box labelled joins, backfills, monitors and on-call pages.

p3-w20-m4.title: Resampling moved the operating point, not the ranking
p3-w20-m4.alt: Five average-precision intervals on one axis where the untreated baseline at 0.4927 sits furthest right and every resampling treatment down to random undersampling at 0.3524 sits left of it, beside a Brier-score ladder rising 18.9-fold from 0.0082 to 0.1548, the cost-matrix threshold arithmetic giving 8 over 608 equals 0.01316, a crossed-out maximise-F1 box, and realised-cost bars in which the untreated model at a tuned threshold is the cheapest at GBP 91,232.

p3-w20-m5.title: The silent version failure is the dangerous one
p3-w20-m5.alt: One fitted pipeline object drawn as nested boxes crosses a dashed version wall from scikit-learn 1.9.0 to 1.5.2 by three arrows: logistic regression ends in a loud AttributeError, random forest loads with a zero prediction difference, and HistGradientBoosting loads silently wrong with a prediction difference of 1.525e-01 circled in red; below, a latency bar splits 5.127 milliseconds into preprocessing and model time against a batched 0.0103 milliseconds per row, and a PSI ruler places three drift measurements against the 0.10 and 0.25 thresholds.

p3-w21-m1.title: The hidden layer re-draws the paper
p3-w21-m1.alt: Four frames: the four XOR points on a unit square with three dashed red straight lines that each misclassify a point, the same square with two deliberate lines h1 and h2 drawn on it, the same four points re-plotted in h1-h2 coordinates where the two positive points land on top of each other and one green line separates them, and the resulting two-input two-hidden-unit network with weights plus one, biases minus 0.5 and minus 1.5 and a minus-one output edge, nine parameters in all, beside a crossed-out no-activation version that collapses back to one line.

p3-w21-m2.title: Store it going forward, multiply it coming back
p3-w21-m2.alt: A six-node computation graph running left to right in blue from x through a matmul giving z1 equals 0.6 and 0.1, a ReLU, a second matmul giving z2 equals 0.7, a sigmoid giving 0.6682 and a binary cross-entropy giving loss 0.4032, with an amber dashed cached box under each intermediate, and five numbered green arrows running right to left underneath carrying the local derivatives, with the sigmoid-plus-cross-entropy simplification to y-hat minus y equals -0.3318 circled and a crossed-out naive recompute-per-weight alternative.

p3-w21-m3.title: Hold the per-layer variance factor at one
p3-w21-m3.alt: A stack of twenty layer bars beside three signal-width ribbons: a Gaussian initialisation flaring outward to a standard deviation of 3.1e6 and then NaN, Xavier on ReLU tapering to a hairline at 1.2e-3 by layer twenty with the arithmetic 0.707 to the twentieth equals one over 1024 left visible, and He initialisation holding constant width at 0.87, with layer-one gradient norms of 4.7e-6 against 1.9e-2 and four small inset loss-curve shapes.

p3-w21-m4.title: Adam buys steps with two numbers per parameter
p3-w21-m4.alt: A narrow elliptical valley crossed by three descent paths - plain SGD zig-zagging violently, momentum damping it to about fourteen steps, and Adam running almost straight down the floor in four - beside a vertical stacked memory bar for a seven-billion-parameter fine-tune with bf16 weights and gradients at 13.5 GB each, an fp32 master copy and two Adam moment buffers at 27 GB each and 30.6 GB of activations, totalling 141 GB, cut by red dashed lines at the 24 GB and 80 GB card limits.

p3-w21-m5.title: Five lines, five silent ways to be wrong
p3-w21-m5.alt: The PyTorch training step drawn as five numbered stations - zero_grad, forward, loss, backward and step - with a big return arrow closing the loop and an amber annotation on each naming its characteristic silent failure, beside a separate evaluation block where model.eval and inference_mode are ticked and their wrong versions struck out, a crossed-out resume that loads the state dict without the optimizer, and bars comparing 41.2 against 27.8 milliseconds per step.

p3-w22-m1.title: Four silent changes between the file and the tensor
p3-w22-m1.alt: A JPEG file becoming a NumPy array of shape 240 by 320 by 3 in BGR uint8, then four stacked blue transformation arrows for channel order, axis order, dtype and normalization, each annotated in red with the bug that skipping it produces, ending in a 3 by 224 by 224 float tensor; below, a five-by-five grid of numbers with a red three-by-three kernel window over its corner producing the value 16 in a three-by-three feature map, with the multiply-accumulate written out longhand.

p3-w22-m2.title: The same nine numbers, at every position
p3-w22-m2.alt: A three-by-three kernel drawn over a five-by-five grid and again one step to the right with a dashed trail, filling two cells of a feature map, beside a struck-out fully-connected alternative at 77,070,336 parameters against the convolution's 896; below, an eight-stage shape ladder from 3 by 224 by 224 to four classes through global average pooling, and a plain block whose layer-one gradient is 2.1e-5 beside a residual block with an identity arc whose layer-one gradient is 4.3e-3, 205 times larger.

p3-w22-m3.title: Slide the gradients into the window, then slide them back
p3-w22-m3.alt: A hand-drawn logarithmic magnitude axis from 1e-10 to 1e5 with a wide dashed BF16 band above it and a narrower hachured FP16 band from 6.1e-5 to 65504, a histogram of gradient magnitudes sitting mostly to the left of the FP16 band in red with 47 percent rounding to zero, a fat amber arrow multiplying by 65536 to move the histogram inside the band leaving 0.02 percent lost, a return arrow for unscaling, a crossed-out clip-before-unscale box, and bars comparing 1,381 against 2,918 images per second.

p3-w22-m4.title: Freeze the body, train the sliver
p3-w22-m4.alt: A diagram split by a dashed line: on the left a hachured padlocked ResNet stack of 11.7 million frozen parameters under a small bright Linear head of 2,052 trainable parameters, 0.018 percent of the model; on the right thirty-two hachured frozen Llama layers totalling 6.74 billion parameters with thin LoRA B and A adapter pairs beside four of them at 0.25 percent, joined by a fat double-headed arrow labelled SAME THING, plus a small chart where the feature-extraction and full-fine-tuning curves cross at about seven hundred images.

p3-w22-m5.title: Cut the head off and it becomes an encoder
p3-w22-m5.alt: A ResNet stack with a red dashed scissor cut between global average pooling and the classification head, leaving a 512-dimensional embedding that feeds a scatter cloud of fifty thousand indexed vectors where a query's three nearest neighbours are circled, beside a table comparing exact Flat, HNSW and IVF-PQ indexes at 2.1, 0.31 and 0.18 milliseconds and recall 1.000, 0.982 and 0.871, and a bottom strip where an image encoder and a text encoder converge on the same index.

p3-w23-m1.title: One process of shared state, or two that share an artifact
p3-w23-m1.alt: On the left a notebook page of numbered cells up to forty-seven with red backward arrows showing out-of-order execution, sitting inside a dashed blob labelled kernel state, and a struck-out arrow running the notebook in production; on the right, across a dashed boundary, train.py and predict.py share only a versioned artifact whose manifest lists model.onnx, classes.json, preprocess_version, git_sha, metrics.json and input_schema, plus one circled preprocess.py imported by both, and bars comparing 3,140 MB of training dependencies with 466 MB of serving dependencies.

p3-w23-m2.title: Five configuration decisions, 68x throughput
p3-w23-m2.alt: Five numbered serving configurations as boxes with proportional throughput bars beside them, climbing from a model loaded inside the handler at 2.3 requests per second and a p99 of 1,840 milliseconds, through an async def that blocks the event loop at 43, a threadpool fighting itself at 58, four uvicorn workers at 97 with p99 61 milliseconds, to micro-batching at 156 with p99 94; the first three are struck through and annotated with the specific mistake, and a bottom row contrasts liveness and readiness endpoints with a database-checking readiness probe crossed out.

p3-w23-m3.title: The order of the instructions is the size of the image
p3-w23-m3.alt: Two stacks of Docker layers drawn to scale - a 3,140 MB naive stack whose pip-install layer alone is 1,455 MB, and a 466 MB ordered stack - joined by a fat amber arrow annotated with five changes and their individual savings from .dockerignore at minus 250 MB to using ONNX instead of torch at minus 851 MB, plus two rebuild timelines showing 214 seconds struck out against 11 seconds, and a crossed-out attempt to shrink an image by deleting files in a later layer.

p3-w23-m4.title: The gate a model pipeline is missing
p3-w23-m4.alt: A nine-gate CI pipeline drawn left to right with each gate's duration underneath and a dashed parallel track carrying two concurrent jobs that rejoin before deploy, cutting the critical path from 4m42s to 3m03s; the fourth gate is drawn heavier and circled as a model quality check, shown twice as a tilting balance comparing a committed baseline of 0.938 against builds of 0.931, which passes, and 0.918, which fails, plus a crossed-out long-lived secret replaced by OIDC and a rollback arrow to a previous image digest.

p3-w23-m5.title: Serverless is cheap until a number you can compute
p3-w23-m5.alt: A log-log chart with a rising Lambda cost line passing $0.10 at a thousand requests a day and $9.73 at a hundred thousand, crossing a flat $12.26 always-on VM line at a circled 126,000 requests per day, beside an inset of cold-start bars falling from 8.7 seconds at 2,100 MB to 1.9 seconds at 280 MB and a second inset where latency falls from 152 to 27 milliseconds as memory rises while cost stays nearly flat, plus crossed-out boxes for provisioned concurrency at $21.90 a month and for GPU models.

p3-w24-m1.title: You write down what should be true
p3-w24-m1.alt: A six-step numbered chain from kubectl apply through the API server into etcd, out to the controllers and scheduler and down to the kubelet, with a struck-out ssh-and-docker-run shortcut beside it, next to a large dashed reconciliation loop whose four stations are desired state, observe actual, diff and act; below, an honest four-row decision table ending in Kubernetes only for many services across many teams, and five broken-pod boxes labelled ImagePullBackOff, OOMKilled, CrashLoopBackOff, CreateContainerConfigError and Pending Insufficient cpu.

p3-w24-m2.title: Two clocks start at once, and neither waits
p3-w24-m2.alt: A thirty-second timeline with two swimlanes that both begin when a pod is marked for deletion: above it the process runs a preStop hook for five seconds, drains for two and exits at seven, with SIGKILL waiting at thirty; below it the EndpointSlice controller removes the pod at 0.1 seconds and kube-proxy on three nodes catches up at 0.9, 1.2 and 3.4 seconds. A red dashed line at 0.3 seconds marks where a naive process exits, losing 187 requests, and a green dashed line at seven seconds loses none of 22,500.

p3-w24-m3.title: Six waiting rooms between load and capacity
p3-w24-m3.alt: A sixty-second timeline where load steps from 10 to 200 requests per second at zero, followed by six hachured waiting-room blocks laid end to end - metrics staleness 12.5 seconds, HPA sync 7.5, scheduling 0.3, container start and warm-up 3.3, readiness probe 2.5 and endpoint propagation 1.2 - bracketed as a predicted median of 27.3 seconds against a measured 31, with a dashed cold-image-pull block adding fourteen, a p99 latency curve spiking and only recovering at the end, a CPU quota bar half filled and half marked THROTTLED, and a comparison showing in-flight requests leading CPU utilisation.

p3-w24-m4.title: Hold the requests back, then multiply once
p3-w24-m4.alt: On the left eight arriving requests each get their own 23-millisecond forward pass at p99 94 milliseconds and 156 requests per second; on the right the same eight are held in a five-millisecond batch window and run as one 31-millisecond pass at p99 78 and 289 rps, with 5.9 times fewer kernel launches; below, a three-by-three grid of measured throughput and p99 for two serving stacks at batch sizes one, eight and thirty-two with the batch-32 TF Serving cell circled at 2.3x, payload bars for REST JSON, gRPC and base64 JPEG, and a shadow-traffic sketch.

p3-w24-m5.title: Four green gauges and a model that has quietly failed
p3-w24-m5.alt: Four ticked golden-signal gauges - p99 61 milliseconds, 97 requests per second, zero errors, 41 percent CPU - feeding a large word GREEN, separated by a thick red line labelled nothing connects these from a model box reading accuracy 93.8 percent falling to 89.6; below, a fifth larger amber distribution gauge holds two overlaid histograms at PSI 0.31, two clock faces compare 41 minutes of drift detection against 3.1 days for labels, and a burn-rate fuel bar carries four alert arrows of different thickness from 14.4x paging down to 1x ticketing, beside a struck-out static latency alert.

p4-w25-m1.title: BPE: the merge table IS the tokenizer
p4-w25-m1.alt: A four-step hand-drawn sequence in which the string 'low lower lowest' is written one box per byte, the most frequent adjacent pair 'lo' is counted and fused, then fused again into 'low', while a merge table on the right grows from the 256 raw byte entries to entries 256 and 257 and the words 'lower' and 'lowest' end up spelled from those merges; underneath, four bars compare gpt2, cl100k_base, Llama 3 and o200k_base on the same ten megabytes of Wikipedia, with a crossed-out word-level tokenizer below them.

p4-w25-m2.title: Embeddings: a lookup, then position added on top
